column3: The United States. The name is 美 plus 国 "country". 美国人 is "an American", and 美语 "American English" is a common name in Taiwan for the English language. In a sentence it works like any place: 去美国 "go to the United States".
column9: The United States. The name is 美 plus 國 "country". 美國人 is "an American", and 美語 "American English" is a common name in Taiwan for the English language. In a sentence it works like any place: 去美國 "go to the United States".

column3: Japan, written with the characters for "sun" and "origin". 日本人 is a Japanese person and 日文 or 日语 the language. It works like any place name in a sentence: 去日本 "go to Japan", 在日本 "in Japan".
column6: Wǒ xià ge yuè qù Rìběn.
column7: I am going to Japan next month.
column9: Japan, written with the characters for "sun" and "origin". 日本人 is a Japanese person and 日文 or 日語 the language. It works like any place name in a sentence: 去日本 "go to Japan", 在日本 "in Japan".

column3: Taiwan. In Taiwan the first character is written either 台 or 台; 台 is the formal form, 台 the everyday one, and both are correct. 台湾人 is a Taiwanese person, 台湾话 usually means Taiwanese Hokkien, not Mandarin (that is 中文, or more formally 国语 or 华语).
column9: Taiwan. In Taiwan the first character is written either 台 or 臺; 臺 is the formal form, 台 the everyday one, and both are correct. 台灣人 is a Taiwanese person, 台灣話 usually means Taiwanese Hokkien, not Mandarin (that is 中文, or more formally 國語 or 華語).

column3: Older sister. In Taiwan both 姊姊 and 姐姐 are written and both are fine; the mainland writes 姐姐. It is the same word, and in speech many people say jiějie. Younger sister is 妹妹, and for sisters in order people say 大姊, 二姊.
column7: My older sister works at a bank.
column9: Older sister. In Taiwan both 姊姊 and 姐姐 are written and both are fine; the mainland writes 姐姐. It is the same word, and in speech many people say jiějie. Younger sister is 妹妹, and for sisters in order people say 大姊, 二姊.

column3: Older sister. In speech it is often used alone after a pronoun: 我姐 "my sister", 你姐 "your sister" (他姐 is rarer). 姊妹 means "sisters" (older and younger), and 大姊, 二姊 count the sisters in order. Taiwan writes both 姊 and 姐.
column9: Older sister. In speech it is often used alone after a pronoun: 我姐 "my sister", 你姐 "your sister" (他姐 is rarer). 姊妹 means "sisters" (older and younger), and 大姊, 二姊 count the sisters in order. Taiwan writes both 姊 and 姐.

column3: Child, the usual word for a young child. 小朋友 is a friendlier word used to or about children. The measure word is 个: 两个小孩 "two children". It is also used for "kids" in a family: 你有小孩吗？ "Do you have children?"
column9: Child, the usual word for a young child. 小朋友 is a friendlier word used to or about children. The measure word is 個: 兩個小孩 "two children". It is also used for "kids" in a family: 你有小孩嗎？ "Do you have children?"

column3: Child, the same word as 小孩 with a suffix 子. 小孩子 sounds a little more spoken and warmer. It is also used to scold or excuse: 小孩子不懂 "he is only a child, he does not understand". Say 一个小孩子 for "a child".
column9: Child, the same word as 小孩 with a suffix 子. 小孩子 sounds a little more spoken and warmer. It is also used to scold or excuse: 小孩子不懂 "he is only a child, he does not understand". Say 一個小孩子 for "a child".

column3: Long (in time). It is about how long something lasts: 很久 "a long time", 多久 "how long", 好久不见 "long time no see". It follows the verb: 我等了很久 "I waited a long time". It is not used for length of objects, which is 长.
column9: Long (in time). It is about how long something lasts: 很久 "a long time", 多久 "how long", 好久不見 "long time no see". It follows the verb: 我等了很久 "I waited a long time". It is not used for length of objects, which is 長.

column3: City bus. 公车 is the everyday word in Taiwan, and 公车站 is a bus stop. The mainland says 公交车 or 公共汽车. Take it with 坐: 坐公车 "ride the bus".
column7: I take the bus to school every day.
column9: City bus. 公車 is the everyday word in Taiwan, and 公車站 is a bus stop. The mainland says 公交車 or 公共汽車. Take it with 坐: 坐公車 "ride the bus".

column3: Car, or vehicle in general; in everyday Taiwan Mandarin it is the usual word for the family car, where the mainland more often says just 车. The measure word is 辆: 一辆车子. A car's color goes before it: 红色的车子.
column6: Tā de chēzi shì hóngsè de.
column9: Car, or vehicle in general; in everyday Taiwan Mandarin it is the usual word for the family car, where the mainland more often says just 車. The measure word is 輛: 一輛車子. A car's color goes before it: 紅色的車子.

column3: Easy. 很容易 "very easy", and 不容易 is "not easy", which often means "difficult": 不容易学 "not easy to learn". The opposite is 难. Put the verb before it: 容易学, 容易忘 "easy to forget".
column7: Chinese is not easy to learn.
column9: Easy. 很容易 "very easy", and 不容易 is "not easy", which often means "difficult": 不容易學 "not easy to learn". The opposite is 難. Put the verb before it: 容易學, 容易忘 "easy to forget".

column3: Sunday. In Taiwan 礼拜 is a common, spoken word for "week", so 礼拜一 is Monday and 礼拜天 Sunday. 星期天 and 星期日 mean the same, and 星期 is the mainland's usual word. 礼拜 "week" also counts weeks: 两个礼拜 "two weeks".
column7: On Sunday we are going hiking.
column9: Sunday. In Taiwan 禮拜 is a common, spoken word for "week", so 禮拜一 is Monday and 禮拜天 Sunday. 星期天 and 星期日 mean the same, and 星期 is the mainland's usual word. 禮拜 "week" also counts weeks: 兩個禮拜 "two weeks".

column3: Fat, plump. It is blunt: telling an adult 你胖了 "you have put on weight" is impolite in most company. Use it for yourself or a pet. 变胖 means "get fat", and the opposite is 瘦. It describes a person's body; for fat on meat the word is 肥.
column9: Fat, plump. It is blunt: telling an adult 你胖了 "you have put on weight" is impolite in most company. Use it for yourself or a pet. 變胖 means "get fat", and the opposite is 瘦. It describes a person's body; for fat on meat the word is 肥.

column3: Short in height, the opposite of 高: 他比我矮 "he is shorter than me". It is used for people, buildings and plants, but not for a short length of something, which is 短. 矮子 is an insulting word for a short person; avoid it.
column7: My younger brother is shorter than me.
column9: Short in height, the opposite of 高: 他比我矮 "he is shorter than me". It is used for people, buildings and plants, but not for a short length of something, which is 短. 矮子 is an insulting word for a short person; avoid it.

column3: Thin, the opposite of 胖. It is a common word for a slim body and is not rude: 你好瘦 "you are so thin". 瘦 also describes meat: 瘦肉 "lean meat". With 了 it shows change: 瘦了 "have got thinner".
column7: She is both tall and thin.
column9: Thin, the opposite of 胖. It is a common word for a slim body and is not rude: 你好瘦 "you are so thin". 瘦 also describes meat: 瘦肉 "lean meat". With 了 it shows change: 瘦了 "have got thinner".

column3: Hour (length of time), a spoken word: 两个钟头 "two hours". 小时 means the same and is common in writing and careful speech. For a time on the clock use 点: 三点. Counts with 个: 一个钟头 or 半个钟头 "half an hour".
column6: Wǒ děng le liǎng ge zhōngtóu.
column9: Hour (length of time), a spoken word: 兩個鐘頭 "two hours". 小時 means the same and is common in writing and careful speech. For a time on the clock use 點: 三點. Counts with 個: 一個鐘頭 or 半個鐘頭 "half an hour".

column3: The year after next. The row of year words goes 前年 "the year before last", 去年, 今年, 明年, 后年. Like other time words it goes before the verb, or first in the sentence. 后年 differs from 后来 "later", which is not a fixed time.
column7: I will go to Taiwan the year after next.
column9: The year after next. The row of year words goes 前年 "the year before last", 去年, 今年, 明年, 後年. Like other time words it goes before the verb, or first in the sentence. 後年 differs from 後來 "later", which is not a fixed time.

column3: Beautiful, more for looks and scenery, as 风景很美 "the view is lovely" or 她很美 "she is beautiful". Longer forms are 美丽 "beautiful" and 漂亮 "pretty". It is also the first character of 美国.
column9: Beautiful, more for looks and scenery, as 風景很美 "the view is lovely" or 她很美 "she is beautiful". Longer forms are 美麗 "beautiful" and 漂亮 "pretty". It is also the first character of 美國.

column3: Found mostly in 应该 "should, ought to": 你应该早点睡 "you should sleep earlier". It is read yīng there. The same character is read yìng in 回应 "respond" and 应用 "apply", a different word. 应该 goes before the verb, and 不应该 means "should not".
column7: You should go to bed earlier.
column9: Found mostly in 應該 "should, ought to": 你應該早點睡 "you should sleep earlier". It is read yīng there. The same character is read yìng in 回應 "respond" and 應用 "apply", a different word. 應該 goes before the verb, and 不應該 means "should not".

column3: Doctor, the formal title. 王医师 is "Dr. Wang", as on hospital notices and name cards. In everyday speech 医生 is more common. 师 also ends other titles for professionals, such as 老师 "teacher".
column9: Doctor, the formal title. 王醫師 is "Dr. Wang", as on hospital notices and name cards. In everyday speech 醫生 is more common. 師 also ends other titles for professionals, such as 老師 "teacher".

column3: A little, a bit, for an amount: 一点水 "a little water", 吃一点 "eat a bit". After an adjective it softens a request or a comparison: 大一点 "a bit bigger", 便宜一点 "a bit cheaper". 点 is also "o'clock", so 一点 can mean "one o'clock".
column7: I'd like to drink a little water.
column9: A little, a bit, for an amount: 一點水 "a little water", 吃一點 "eat a bit". After an adjective it softens a request or a comparison: 大一點 "a bit bigger", 便宜一點 "a bit cheaper". 點 is also "o'clock", so 一點 can mean "one o'clock".

column3: The measure word for flat things you can spread out: 一张纸 "a sheet of paper", 两张票 "two tickets", 一张桌子 "a table", 一张床 "a bed", and also photographs. It also appears as a very common surname, Zhāng.
column6: Wǒ mǎi le liǎng zhāng piào.
column9: The measure word for flat things you can spread out: 一張紙 "a sheet of paper", 兩張票 "two tickets", 一張桌子 "a table", 一張床 "a bed", and also photographs. It also appears as a very common surname, Zhāng.

column3: Restaurant, usually a larger sit-down place with a menu or a hotel's dining room. 餐馆 and 饭馆 are also used, and 小吃店 is a small eatery. The measure word is 家: 一家餐厅. 厅 also appears in 客厅 "living room".
column6: Zhè jiā cāntīng de cài hěn hǎochī.
column7: The food at this restaurant is very good.
column9: Restaurant, usually a larger sit-down place with a menu or a hotel's dining room. 餐館 and 飯館 are also used, and 小吃店 is a small eatery. The measure word is 家: 一家餐廳. 廳 also appears in 客廳 "living room".

column3: Read aloud and "study". In Taiwan 念书 means "study, go to school", and 念大学 "attend university". For reading a text aloud, Taiwan writes 念 or 念, and both are fine. For "miss someone", only 念 is used: 想念你. The thing read comes after: 念课文 "read the text aloud".
column9: Read aloud and "study". In Taiwan 念書 means "study, go to school", and 念大學 "attend university". For reading a text aloud, Taiwan writes 念 or 唸, and both are fine. For "miss someone", only 念 is used: 想念你. The thing read comes after: 念課文 "read the text aloud".

column3: The measure word for long thin things, above all pens and flowers: 一枝笔 "a pen", 一枝花 "a flower". Taiwan commonly writes 枝 here, where the mainland usually writes 支. Its other meaning is "branch".
column9: The measure word for long thin things, above all pens and flowers: 一枝筆 "a pen", 一枝花 "a flower". Taiwan commonly writes 枝 here, where the mainland usually writes 支. Its other meaning is "branch".

column3: Cow, ox, cattle. It is also the base of 牛肉 "beef" and 牛奶 "milk", and 牛肉面 "beef noodle soup" is a famous dish in Taiwan. As a measure it is 一头牛 or 一只牛; 头 is more usual for cattle.
column9: Cow, ox, cattle. It is also the base of 牛肉 "beef" and 牛奶 "milk", and 牛肉麵 "beef noodle soup" is a famous dish in Taiwan. As a measure it is 一頭牛 or 一隻牛; 頭 is more usual for cattle.

column3: Pig, and 猪肉 is "pork". The measure word is 只: 一只猪. A pig is also a common insult for a greedy or lazy person, so do not call someone 猪.
column9: Pig, and 豬肉 is "pork". The measure word is 隻: 一隻豬. A pig is also a common insult for a greedy or lazy person, so do not call someone 豬.

column3: Schoolwork, homework: 做功课 "do homework", 写功课 "write homework". 作业 means the same, and both are common in schools; 功课 is not used for a job's work, which is 工作.
column7: I haven't finished my homework yet.
column9: Schoolwork, homework: 做功課 "do homework", 寫功課 "write homework". 作業 means the same, and both are common in schools; 功課 is not used for a job's work, which is 工作.

column3: Room, house. It is mostly part of a longer word: 房间 "room", 房子 "house, apartment", 房租 "rent", 房东 "landlord". On its own, it is seen in signs and set phrases more than in speech. 房子 is the everyday word for a home you buy or rent.
column7: I am looking for a place to live.
column9: Room, house. It is mostly part of a longer word: 房間 "room", 房子 "house, apartment", 房租 "rent", 房東 "landlord". On its own, it is seen in signs and set phrases more than in speech. 房子 is the everyday word for a home you buy or rent.

column3: Table, desk, almost always in 桌子, or 书桌 "desk", 餐桌 "dining table". The measure word is 张: 一张桌子. Things sit on a table with 在…上 or 在…上面: 书在桌子上. 桌 on its own turns up mainly in compounds.
column7: The book is on the table.
column9: Table, desk, almost always in 桌子, or 書桌 "desk", 餐桌 "dining table". The measure word is 張: 一張桌子. Things sit on a table with 在…上 or 在…上面: 書在桌子上. 桌 on its own turns up mainly in compounds.

column3: Chair, normally in 椅子, with 张 as measure word like a table: 一张椅子. Sit on one with 坐: 坐在椅子上.
column9: Chair, normally in 椅子, with 張 as measure word like a table: 一張椅子. Sit on one with 坐: 坐在椅子上.

column3: Flower, with the spoken ending 儿. That ending is a northern, mainland habit; in Taiwan the word is simply 花, and 花儿 mainly shows up in songs and poems. The measure word is 朵 for a flower, 束 for a bunch, and 枝 for a single stem.
column6: Yuànzi lǐ de huār kāi le.
column7: The flowers in the yard have bloomed.
column9: Flower, with the spoken ending 兒. That ending is a northern, mainland habit; in Taiwan the word is simply 花, and 花兒 mainly shows up in songs and poems. The measure word is 朵 for a flower, 束 for a bunch, and 枝 for a single stem.

column3: Coffee. The word is a sound loan from the foreign word, which is why the two characters are not about meaning. 咖啡店 and 咖啡厅 are cafés. Count it with 杯: 一杯咖啡 "a cup of coffee". 喝咖啡 is the verb phrase.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng hē yī bēi kāfēi.
column7: I'd like a cup of coffee.
column9: Coffee. The word is a sound loan from the foreign word, which is why the two characters are not about meaning. 咖啡店 and 咖啡廳 are cafés. Count it with 杯: 一杯咖啡 "a cup of coffee". 喝咖啡 is the verb phrase.

column3: Every, each. It is followed by a measure word or time word: 每天 "every day", 每个人 "everyone", 每次 "every time". 每 + noun often goes with 都 later in the sentence: 每个人都来了 "everyone came".
column9: Every, each. It is followed by a measure word or time word: 每天 "every day", 每個人 "everyone", 每次 "every time". 每 + noun often goes with 都 later in the sentence: 每個人都來了 "everyone came".

column3: Play, have fun, for leisure not sports: 去玩 "go out and have fun", 玩游戏 "play a game", 好玩 "fun". In a question about plans, 去哪里玩 "where to go for fun" is natural. You can also play with objects: 玩手机 "mess around on your phone". Competitive sports use 打, not 玩.
column6: Zhōumò nǐ xiǎng qù nǎlǐ wán?
column7: Where do you want to go for fun this weekend?
column9: Play, have fun, for leisure not sports: 去玩 "go out and have fun", 玩遊戲 "play a game", 好玩 "fun". In a question about plans, 去哪裡玩 "where to go for fun" is natural. You can also play with objects: 玩手機 "mess around on your phone". Competitive sports use 打, not 玩.

column3: Jump: 跳高 "high jump", 跳起来 "jump up". It is also the first half of 跳舞 "dance", and 心跳 is "heartbeat". Degree comes after 得: 他跳得很高 "he jumps very high".
column9: Jump: 跳高 "high jump", 跳起來 "jump up". It is also the first half of 跳舞 "dance", and 心跳 is "heartbeat". Degree comes after 得: 他跳得很高 "he jumps very high".

column3: Dance. 跳舞 is a verb plus object, so the verb is repeated when you give a degree: 跳舞跳得很好, or put 舞 first: 舞跳得很好. 她会跳舞 "she can dance". Also 跳一支舞 "dance a dance".
column9: Dance. 跳舞 is a verb plus object, so the verb is repeated when you give a degree: 跳舞跳得很好, or put 舞 first: 舞跳得很好. 她會跳舞 "she can dance". Also 跳一支舞 "dance a dance".

column3: Thing, matter, with the northern 儿 ending, common on the mainland. Taiwan says 事 or 事情: 有事 "have something to do", 没事 "nothing's wrong". 你有什么事儿吗 sounds northern or mainland to Taiwan ears; in Taiwan you would more likely hear 你有什么事吗.
column9: Thing, matter, with the northern 兒 ending, common on the mainland. Taiwan says 事 or 事情: 有事 "have something to do", 沒事 "nothing's wrong". 你有什麼事兒嗎 sounds northern or mainland to Taiwan ears; in Taiwan you would more likely hear 你有什麼事嗎.

column3: Inside. It follows the place: 房间里面 "in the room", and often just 里: 房间里. It can also stand by itself: 里面有人吗 "is anyone in there?". The opposite is 外面.
column7: There is money in the wallet.
column9: Inside. It follows the place: 房間裡面 "in the room", and often just 裡: 房間裡. It can also stand by itself: 裡面有人嗎 "is anyone in there?". The opposite is 外面.

column3: Above, on top, and also "the above part". 桌子上面 "on the table", 上面的人 "the person above". Same pattern as 下面, 里面 and 外面. As in English, it can mean "the above-mentioned" in writing: 上面说的 "what was said above".
column7: The book is on the table.
column9: Above, on top, and also "the above part". 桌子上面 "on the table", 上面的人 "the person above". Same pattern as 下面, 裡面 and 外面. As in English, it can mean "the above-mentioned" in writing: 上面說的 "what was said above".

column3: Below, underneath, and "the next part". 椅子下面 "under the chair". 下面 can also mean what follows: 下面请看 "please look at what follows". Short form is 下: 桌子下.
column7: The cat is under the chair.
column9: Below, underneath, and "the next part". 椅子下面 "under the chair". 下面 can also mean what follows: 下面請看 "please look at what follows". Short form is 下: 桌子下.

column3: Outside: 外面 is the usual word, as in 外面很冷 "it is cold outside" or 在外面等 "wait outside". People also say 外头, which is more spoken. It is the opposite of 里面. 外面 can also mean "away from home": 在外面吃饭 "eat out".
column9: Outside: 外面 is the usual word, as in 外面很冷 "it is cold outside" or 在外面等 "wait outside". People also say 外頭, which is more spoken. It is the opposite of 裡面. 外面 can also mean "away from home": 在外面吃飯 "eat out".

column3: Outside, the spoken version of 外面, where 头 is light. Both are used with little difference: 外头很冷, 在外头等. 头 as a suffix also forms 里头 "inside", 前头 "ahead" and 后头 "behind". It can sound a bit more colloquial.
column6: Wàitou hěn lěng, duō chuān yīdiǎn.
column9: Outside, the spoken version of 外面, where 頭 is light. Both are used with little difference: 外頭很冷, 在外頭等. 頭 as a suffix also forms 裡頭 "inside", 前頭 "ahead" and 後頭 "behind". It can sound a bit more colloquial.

column3: In front, ahead, and also "earlier (in a text)". 前面有一家店 "there is a shop ahead". In notices 前方 is also used. The opposite is 后面. A convenience store is a 便利商店 in Taiwan; the mainland says 便利店.
column6: Qiánmiàn yǒu yī jiā biànlì shāngdiàn.
column7: There is a convenience store ahead.
column9: In front, ahead, and also "earlier (in a text)". 前面有一家店 "there is a shop ahead". In notices 前方 is also used. The opposite is 後面. A convenience store is a 便利商店 in Taiwan; the mainland says 便利店.

column3: Behind, at the back. 在…后面 "behind …", and 后面 also means the part that comes later: 后面还有 "there is more after this". The 面 is light here, as in 后面 hòumian. Opposite of 前面.
column7: The school is behind the park.
column9: Behind, at the back. 在…後面 "behind …", and 後面 also means the part that comes later: 後面還有 "there is more after this". The 面 is light here, as in 後面 hòumian. Opposite of 前面.

column3: Side, beside, used in compounds more than alone: 旁边 "beside, next to", 路旁 "roadside". 他坐在我旁边 "he sits next to me". In speech, 旁边 is the usual word. 旁人 means "bystanders".
column9: Side, beside, used in compounds more than alone: 旁邊 "beside, next to", 路旁 "roadside". 他坐在我旁邊 "he sits next to me". In speech, 旁邊 is the usual word. 旁人 means "bystanders".

column3: Place. It takes a describing word before it: 好地方 "a good place", 什么地方 "what place", 这个地方 "this place". 你住什么地方？ "where do you live?" is a question with it, though 哪里 is the more common question word.
column9: Place. It takes a describing word before it: 好地方 "a good place", 什麼地方 "what place", 這個地方 "this place". 你住什麼地方？ "where do you live?" is a question with it, though 哪裡 is the more common question word.

column3: Nearby, in the neighborhood: 学校附近 "near the school", 这附近 "around here". Put it after the place: 公园附近. Also 附近的 plus noun: 附近的商店 "the nearby shops". It is used for areas, not for exact distance.
column7: Is there a bank around here?
column9: Nearby, in the neighborhood: 學校附近 "near the school", 這附近 "around here". Put it after the place: 公園附近. Also 附近的 plus noun: 附近的商店 "the nearby shops". It is used for areas, not for exact distance.

column3: Taxi, the standard word in Taiwan. It is made of 计程 "measure the distance" and 车, for the meter; the mainland says 出租车, and Hong Kong 的士. Cabs in Taiwan are famous yellow, and people often call them 小黄. You take one with 坐 and call one with 叫: 叫计程车.
column9: Taxi, the standard word in Taiwan. It is made of 計程 "measure the distance" and 車, for the meter; the mainland says 出租車, and Hong Kong 的士. Cabs in Taiwan are famous yellow, and people often call them 小黃. You take one with 坐 and call one with 叫: 叫計程車.

column3: Nose, mostly in compounds, with 鼻子 the word used alone. With a cold, 流鼻水 is a runny nose and 鼻塞 a stuffy nose. 鼻涕 is the thicker snot; Taiwan uses both words, for different things.
column9: Nose, mostly in compounds, with 鼻子 the word used alone. With a cold, 流鼻水 is a runny nose and 鼻塞 a stuffy nose. 鼻涕 is the thicker snot; Taiwan uses both words, for different things.

column3: Nose. The suffix 子 makes it a free word: 我的鼻子 "my nose". A high-bridged nose is 鼻子高 or 高鼻子. One nose is 一个鼻子. A stuffy nose is 鼻塞.
column9: Nose. The suffix 子 makes it a free word: 我的鼻子 "my nose". A high-bridged nose is 鼻子高 or 高鼻子. One nose is 一個鼻子. A stuffy nose is 鼻塞.

column3: Ear, normally in 耳朵. The measure word is 只 for one ear: 一只耳朵, or 对 for a pair. Parts of the body are said with 的 or without: 我的耳朵 "my ears". 耳朵痛 is "earache".
column9: Ear, normally in 耳朵. The measure word is 隻 for one ear: 一隻耳朵, or 對 for a pair. Parts of the body are said with 的 or without: 我的耳朵 "my ears". 耳朵痛 is "earache".

column3: Catch a cold, and "a cold". 感冒了 "have caught a cold". Both a verb and a noun: 得了感冒, 我感冒了. Symptoms: 流鼻水 "runny nose", 咳嗽 "cough", 发烧 "fever". Medicine: 感冒药.
column6: Wǒ gǎnmào le, tóu hěn tòng.
column7: I have a cold and my head hurts a lot.
column9: Catch a cold, and "a cold". 感冒了 "have caught a cold". Both a verb and a noun: 得了感冒, 我感冒了. Symptoms: 流鼻水 "runny nose", 咳嗽 "cough", 發燒 "fever". Medicine: 感冒藥.

column3: Hurt, ache, the usual word in Taiwan: 头痛 "headache", 肚子痛 "stomachache", 好痛 "it hurts!". The mainland says 疼 more often in speech; both are understood in Taiwan. Place the body part first: 我的肚子痛.
column9: Hurt, ache, the usual word in Taiwan: 頭痛 "headache", 肚子痛 "stomachache", 好痛 "it hurts!". The mainland says 疼 more often in speech; both are understood in Taiwan. Place the body part first: 我的肚子痛.

column3: Mouth, the spoken noun, usually 嘴巴. 嘴 alone is also found in compounds like 嘴唇 "lip". 张开嘴巴 "open your mouth", 闭嘴 "shut up" (rude). The formal word for mouth is 口. 嘴巴 can also mean "speech" informally: 嘴巴很甜 "sweet-talking".
column9: Mouth, the spoken noun, usually 嘴巴. 嘴 alone is also found in compounds like 嘴唇 "lip". 張開嘴巴 "open your mouth", 閉嘴 "shut up" (rude). The formal word for mouth is 口. 嘴巴 can also mean "speech" informally: 嘴巴很甜 "sweet-talking".

column3: Shoes. The measure word is 双 for a pair: 一双鞋子, and 一只 for a single shoe. Types: 运动鞋 "sports shoes", 拖鞋 "slippers", 皮鞋 "leather shoes". People often take their shoes off when entering a home: 脱鞋子. Try: 请脱鞋子.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng mǎi yī shuāng xīn xiézi.
column7: I want to buy a new pair of shoes.
column9: Shoes. The measure word is 雙 for a pair: 一雙鞋子, and 一隻 for a single shoe. Types: 運動鞋 "sports shoes", 拖鞋 "slippers", 皮鞋 "leather shoes". People often take their shoes off when entering a home: 脫鞋子. Try: 請脫鞋子.

column3: Clothes, usually in 衣服 "clothes" (measure word 件: 一件衣服), 上衣 "top", 雨衣 "raincoat". It is a bound form, not used alone in speech. At the left of a character it is cut down to 衤, as in 里, which has the clothing sign.
column7: This piece of clothing looks very nice.
column9: Clothes, usually in 衣服 "clothes" (measure word 件: 一件衣服), 上衣 "top", 雨衣 "raincoat". It is a bound form, not used alone in speech. At the left of a character it is cut down to 衤, as in 裡, which has the clothing sign.

column3: Old for things and for things from the past: 旧衣服 "old clothes", 旧朋友 "old friend" and 旧地方 "the old place". Not for people's age, which is 老. The opposite is 新. The character originally named a kind of owl, and was borrowed for the sound of the word "old".
column6: Zhè shuāng xiézi tài jiù le.
column7: This pair of shoes is too old.
column9: Old for things and for things from the past: 舊衣服 "old clothes", 舊朋友 "old friend" and 舊地方 "the old place". Not for people's age, which is 老. The opposite is 新. The character originally named a kind of owl, and was borrowed for the sound of the word "old".

column3: Together, in total. It is found in 一共 "altogether, in total" (asking the total price: 一共多少钱), 共同 "common, joint", and 公共 "public". Alone it is mostly formal writing. 一共 goes before the verb or number.
column9: Together, in total. It is found in 一共 "altogether, in total" (asking the total price: 一共多少錢), 共同 "common, joint", and 公共 "public". Alone it is mostly formal writing. 一共 goes before the verb or number.

column3: Chopsticks, in 筷子, always plural in use: 一双筷子 "a pair of chopsticks". The older word for chopsticks was 箸, which sounded like 住 "stay, stop", so the name was avoided and 快 "fast" gave the new one. 用筷子吃饭 "eat with chopsticks".
column6: Qǐng gěi wǒ yī shuāng kuàizi.
column7: Please give me a pair of chopsticks.
column9: Chopsticks, in 筷子, always plural in use: 一雙筷子 "a pair of chopsticks". The older word for chopsticks was 箸, which sounded like 住 "stay, stop", so the name was avoided and 快 "fast" gave the new one. 用筷子吃飯 "eat with chopsticks".

column3: A bit, somewhat. It comes before an adjective, usually one you do not like: 有点贵 "a bit expensive", 有点冷 "a bit cold". Compare with 一点 after the adjective: 便宜一点 "a bit cheaper, please". Before a verb: 我有点想家 "I am a little homesick". 有点 is also used by itself to soften: 有点难.
column9: A bit, somewhat. It comes before an adjective, usually one you do not like: 有點貴 "a bit expensive", 有點冷 "a bit cold". Compare with 一點 after the adjective: 便宜一點 "a bit cheaper, please". Before a verb: 我有點想家 "I am a little homesick". 有點 is also used by itself to soften: 有點難.

column3: A little, somewhat, the same as 有点, with 一 in the middle. 我有一点饿 "I am a bit hungry". It can also mean "have a little": 我有一点钱 "I have a bit of money". Before an adjective, it is mildly negative, like 有点. Like 有点, it comes before the adjective.
column9: A little, somewhat, the same as 有點, with 一 in the middle. 我有一點餓 "I am a bit hungry". It can also mean "have a little": 我有一點錢 "I have a bit of money". Before an adjective, it is mildly negative, like 有點. Like 有點, it comes before the adjective.

column3: Snack, small dish: the small foods sold at stalls and night markets, such as 蚵仔煎 "oyster omelet" and 卤肉饭. 夜市小吃 are the snacks of a night market, and 小吃店 is a small restaurant serving them. For packaged snacks the word is 零食.
column7: The night market has a lot of snacks.
column9: Snack, small dish: the small foods sold at stalls and night markets, such as 蚵仔煎 "oyster omelet" and 滷肉飯. 夜市小吃 are the snacks of a night market, and 小吃店 is a small restaurant serving them. For packaged snacks the word is 零食.

column3: Dumpling, usually 饺子. 水饺 "boiled dumplings" are a standard meal, and 锅贴 "pan-fried dumplings" are often sold by the piece. 饺 is normally part of a compound. To eat them: 吃水饺. Count them with 个 or 颗.
column9: Dumpling, usually 餃子. 水餃 "boiled dumplings" are a standard meal, and 鍋貼 "pan-fried dumplings" are often sold by the piece. 餃 is normally part of a compound. To eat them: 吃水餃. Count them with 個 or 顆.

column3: Soup, and "broth". You drink soup in Chinese, 喝汤, and count it with 碗: 一碗汤. Soups are named by their contents: 蛋花汤 "egg-drop soup", 鱼汤 "fish soup".
column6: Wǒ xiǎng hē yī wǎn rè tāng.
column7: I'd like a bowl of hot soup.
column9: Soup, and "broth". You drink soup in Chinese, 喝湯, and count it with 碗: 一碗湯. Soups are named by their contents: 蛋花湯 "egg-drop soup", 魚湯 "fish soup".

column3: Cake: 蛋 "egg" plus 糕, a soft baked or steamed food. 生日蛋糕 is a birthday cake, and 一块蛋糕 is a piece of cake. 糕 also appears in 年糕 and 萝卜糕, steamed foods. A cake shop is a 蛋糕店.
column7: I want to eat birthday cake.
column9: Cake: 蛋 "egg" plus 糕, a soft baked or steamed food. 生日蛋糕 is a birthday cake, and 一塊蛋糕 is a piece of cake. 糕 also appears in 年糕 and 蘿蔔糕, steamed foods. A cake shop is a 蛋糕店.

column3: Banana. The measure word is 根 for a single banana, or 串 for a bunch: 吃一根香蕉. 香 "fragrant" plus 蕉. 香蕉牛奶 "banana milk" is a common drink.
column4: 我每天早上吃一根香蕉。
column5: 我每天早上吃一根香蕉。
column6: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang chī yī gēn xiāngjiāo.
column7: I eat a banana every morning.
column9: Banana. The measure word is 根 for a single banana, or 串 for a bunch: 吃一根香蕉. 香 "fragrant" plus 蕉. 香蕉牛奶 "banana milk" is a common drink.

column3: Drink, beverage. Taiwan's 饮料店 sell tea drinks and are everywhere, like bubble tea shops. Ask 你想喝什么饮料？ for "what do you want to drink?". The mainland says 饮料 too, but also 饮品. Put 喝 in front: 喝饮料. Cold drinks: 冷饮.
column7: What would you like to drink?
column9: Drink, beverage. Taiwan's 飲料店 sell tea drinks and are everywhere, like bubble tea shops. Ask 你想喝什麼飲料？ for "what do you want to drink?". The mainland says 飲料 too, but also 飲品. Put 喝 in front: 喝飲料. Cold drinks: 冷飲.

column3: Fruit juice: 果 "fruit" plus 汁 "juice". Count with 杯: 一杯果汁. Specific juices name the fruit first: 柳橙汁 "orange juice", 西瓜汁 "watermelon juice". 汁 is also found in names like 肉汁 "gravy".
column7: I'd like a glass of juice.
column9: Fruit juice: 果 "fruit" plus 汁 "juice". Count with 杯: 一杯果汁. Specific juices name the fruit first: 柳橙汁 "orange juice", 西瓜汁 "watermelon juice". 汁 is also found in names like 肉汁 "gravy".

column3: Sweet. Also used for things that are very sweet or pleasant: 甜点 "dessert", 甜的 "the sweet one". In drink shops you can choose the sugar: 全糖, 半糖, 微糖, 无糖 "full, half, light, no sugar". Opposite: 苦, 咸.
column6: Zhè bēi yǐnliào tài tián le.
column9: Sweet. Also used for things that are very sweet or pleasant: 甜點 "dessert", 甜的 "the sweet one". In drink shops you can choose the sugar: 全糖, 半糖, 微糖, 無糖 "full, half, light, no sugar". Opposite: 苦, 鹹.

column3: Chocolate, a sound loan from English with the characters 巧克力 chosen for sound. 巧克力蛋糕 is "chocolate cake" and 热巧克力 "hot chocolate". Count with 块: 一块巧克力. The characters are chosen for sound only, not meaning.
column9: Chocolate, a sound loan from English with the characters 巧克力 chosen for sound. 巧克力蛋糕 is "chocolate cake" and 熱巧克力 "hot chocolate". Count with 塊: 一塊巧克力. The characters are chosen for sound only, not meaning.

column3: Ice, and "iced, cold". 冰水 is "ice water" and 冰的 "the cold one". When ordering a drink in Taiwan: 正常冰 "regular ice", 少冰 "less ice", 微冰 "a little ice", 去冰 "no ice". 冰箱 is "refrigerator", and 冰淇淋 "ice cream".
column6: Wǒ yào bīng de, bù yào rè de.
column7: I want the cold one, not the hot one.
column9: Ice, and "iced, cold". 冰水 is "ice water" and 冰的 "the cold one". When ordering a drink in Taiwan: 正常冰 "regular ice", 少冰 "less ice", 微冰 "a little ice", 去冰 "no ice". 冰箱 is "refrigerator", and 冰淇淋 "ice cream".

column3: Side, with the northern ending 儿. In Taiwan people usually say 边 or 旁边, 左边 "left side", 这边 "this side", and keep 边儿 as something heard in northern speech or on the mainland. 路边 is "roadside". The 儿 ending is not written in Taiwan's everyday text.
column7: There is a shop by the road.
column9: Side, with the northern ending 兒. In Taiwan people usually say 邊 or 旁邊, 左邊 "left side", 這邊 "this side", and keep 邊兒 as something heard in northern speech or on the mainland. 路邊 is "roadside". The 兒 ending is not written in Taiwan's everyday text.

column3: Read děi, this is "must, have to": 我得走了 "I have to go". It is spoken and goes before the verb. The negative is not 不得, but 不用 "no need" or 不必. The same character is read dé in 得到 "get" and de in 跑得快 "run fast". For a stronger "must", 必须 is the written word.
column9: Read děi, this is "must, have to": 我得走了 "I have to go". It is spoken and goes before the verb. The negative is not 不得, but 不用 "no need" or 不必. The same character is read dé in 得到 "get" and de in 跑得快 "run fast". For a stronger "must", 必須 is the written word.
